# Simulating data and encoding sampling events

## Catch up

The exercises in this chapter will pick up from where we left of in the chapter
on building _slendr_ demographic models. To catch up, feel free to use the
following script as a basis for what's coming up next:

```{r}
library(slendr)
init_env()

p1 <- population("p1", time = 12000, N = 1000)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 9000, N = 1000, parent = p1)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 6000, N = 1000, parent = p2) %>%
  resize(N = 100, time = 1800) %>%
  resize(N = 2000, time = 1000)
p4 <- population("p4", time = 3000, N = 1000, parent = p3)

gf <- gene_flow(from = p2, to = p3, start = 3000, end = 2200, proportion = 0.1)

model <- compile_model(
    populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4), gene_flow = gf,
    generation_time = 30,
    time_units = "years before present"
)

plot_model(model, proportions = TRUE)
```

:::

### Exercise: Simulating genomic data

Once we have compiled a _slendr_ model and stored it in a variable, we can
finally simulate data from it. By default, a simulation from a _slendr_ model
always produces a [tree-sequence](https://tskit.dev/tutorials/what_is.html)
object as a result. We'll explore the tree-sequence concept in a bit more detail
later, but for now we can treat it as a black box which somehow "magically"
stores genomic variation of a set of individuals.

::: aside

**Note:** As discussed in our introduction to this session, tree sequences
provide an extremely efficient means to store and work with genomic data at a
massive scale. However, you can always get simulated data even in [traditional
file
formats](https://bodkan.net/slendr/reference/index.html#tree-sequence-format-conversion),
such as VCF, EIGENSTRAT, or a plain table of ancestral/derived genotype states.

In this section, we will be only working with tree sequences, because it's much
easier and faster to get interesting statistics from it directly in R, but you
can always compute the same statistics from simulated VCF or EIGENSTRAT files
using any of the available software methods as well.

:::

There are two simulation engines built into _slendr_ implemented by functions
`msprime()` and `slim()`. For traditional, non-spatial, neutral demographic
models, the `msprime()` engine is much more efficient, so we'll be using that
for the time being. However, it's worth noting that from the perspective of
population genetics theory, both simulation functions will give you practicalyl
the same results for any given compiled _slendr_ model (up to some level of
stochastic noise).

::: aside

**Note:** The alternative engine implemented by the `slim()` function plays an
important role for spatial simulations and for simulations of natural selection
--- these are the primary two reasons why it's included in _slendr_ in the first
place.

:::

As we discussed in the introduction, here's how you can use simulate a tree
sequence from a compiled _slendr_ `model`. You will be seeing this kind of
pattern over and over again, so it's worth keeping it in mind any time you will
be simulating data going forward.

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: false
ts <- msprime(
  model,
  sequence_length = <length of the simulated [bp]>,
  recombination_rate = <uniform recombination rate [crossovers per bp per generation]>
)
```

---

**Simulate a tree sequence from your compiled `model` using the `msprime()`
engine and store it in a variable `ts` as shown in the snippet of code right
above. Set the parameters `sequence_length = 1e6` (length of the sequence in bp)
and `recombination_rate = 1e-8` (crossover events per base pair per
generation).**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

This command simulates a _tskit_ tree sequence from a _slendr_ model. Again,
note that we don't have to write any _msprime_ or _tskit_ code to implement the
simulation because _slendr_ does all the work for us!

```{r}
ts <- msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8)
```

:::

**Now type out the `ts` object in the console --- what do you see? Try to relate
some of the information in the presented summary to our overview discussion of
tree sequences. For instance, what are the "nodes" and "edges"? What's the
difference between "samples" and "individuals"? How many "trees" does the tree
sequence have, and how many "mutations" are stored in it?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

Evaluating the `ts` variable in the R console should give you a summary of a
tree-sequence object with some lower-level technical details about the genomic
sequence which it encodes:

```{r}
ts
```

For instance, our tree sequence contains genomic information for `{r}
ts$num_individuals`, each of them diploid. This makes for `{r}ts$num_samples`
samples in total, where a "sample" is a "node" in a tree sequence representing
one haplotype (i.e., one chromosome) of a simulated individual. All other
"nodes" (of which there are many, many more) represent ancestral haplotypes of
these recorded individuals for which we generally have only a part of their
genomic information---a sequence information which made it through recombination
to some of the recorded samples.

:::

::: aside

**Note:** Similarly to the symbol `model`, whenever we from now on refer to
`ts`, we will be talking about some simulated tree-sequence object stored in an
R variable `ts`.

:::

---

In the `ts` summary, you probably noticed there are no mutations! As we will see
later, the magic of tree sequences allows us to compute nearly any conceivable
population genetic statistic even without mutations. That said, particularly for
exploring statistics computed by various third-party software outside of R,
having mutations can be often useful.

**Modify the part of your script which simulates the `ts` object, adding a `%>%
ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)` after the `msprime(...)` function call. After
you execute this new command and type `ts` in the R console to inspect the
summary, you should see that mutations have been added.**

::: aside

**Note:** Even though mutations are generally not needed, there's almost never
any huge downside to adding them, so I recommend you always use both `msprime()`
and `ts_mutate()` in your models.

:::

Here's the general pattern of how we simulate genomic data with _slendr_
including mutations:

```{r}
ts <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)
```

We can see that, indeed, the tree sequence now has `{r} ts$num_mutations`
mutations in it.

---

## Exercise: working with "samples"

If we are to use tree-sequence data for efficient computation of relevant
population genomic statistics, we need a way to refer to individuals and
populations. For this purpose, _slendr_ provides three important functions:
`ts_samples()`, `ts_names()`, and `ts_nodes()`.

At the bare minimum, these functions accept the tree sequence `ts` as their
first argument (i.e., can be run such as `ts_samples(ts)`)**.

---

**Run each of these three functions on your `ts` tree sequence, then try
answering these questions:**

- How many individuals are in your tree sequence based on these functions?

- How is the result of `ts_nodes()` different from `ts_samples()`?

- What are the `time` values of recorded individuals based on the information in
these tables?

- Are the `time` values the same in both?

- How many individuals in total are in the tree sequence based on these two
functions, and how many of them are in each population? Why do you get the
numbers you got, given the model which you programmed and simulated?

- How does `ts_names()` differ from the two table-producing functions?

**Use your _tidyverse_ knowledge to play around with the output of `ts_samples()` and `ts_nodes()` to answer these questions.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

`ts_samples()` gives us a small metadata table with recorded individuals' names,
populations, and times:

```{r}
#| message: false
ts_samples(ts)
ts_samples(ts) %>% nrow()

library(dplyr)
ts_samples(ts) %>% group_by(pop) %>% summarize(n = n())
```

`ts_nodes()` gives us a much larger table about tree-sequence nodes, which
includes not only information about recorded individuals chromosomes (one node,
or chromosome, for each), meaning that we get two rows of the table for each
individual:

```{r}
ts_nodes(ts)

ts_nodes(ts) %>% filter(name == "p1_42")
```

Additionally, the table also contains information about the recorded
individuals' ancestral (unsampled) haplotypes, i.e. individuals who lived in
their genealogical history, but whose complete genomic information we no longer
have (because they mostl likely passed only a subset of their genomes to the
individuals which we simulated or sequenced):

```{r}
ts_nodes(ts) %>% filter(time > 0)
```

```{r}
library(ggplot2)

cowplot::plot_grid(ts_nodes(ts) %>%
  filter(is.na(name)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(time)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
    scale_x_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~is.na(name), scales = "free_x"),
  plot_model(model))
```

## Exercise: Scheduling sampling events

We can see that our tree sequence contains a massive number of individuals. Too
many, in fact --- we recorded every single individual alive at the end of our
simulation, which is something we're unlikely to be ever lucky enough to have,
regardless of which species we study.

To get closer to the scale of the genomic data that we usually work with, we can
restrict our simulation to only record a subset of individuals---we do this
using a process called "scheduling of recorded individuals" implemented by the
_slendr_ function `schedule_sampling()`. Simply speaking, this is a
functionality of _slendr_ which precisely defines which individuals will be
recorded in the tree sequence while ignoring everyone else.

The function follows the structure in the following snippet, representing
another very useful pattern worth keeping in mind going forward:

```{r}
#| eval: false
schedule <- schedule_sampling(
  <compiled slendr model>,
  times = <numbers representing times of recording>,
  list(<population>, <number of samples to record>),
  list(<population>, <number of samples to record>)
  [... etc. ]
)
```

We then use this `schedule` object in a standard `msprime()` function call,
setting it as the argument of the same name, i.e. like this:

```{r}
#| eval: false
ts <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)
```

---

**To get an idea about what this function does in practice, modify the command
which simulates the `ts` object in your script according to the snippet above,
but include a schedule for recording 5 individuals from each of the four
populations. When you run a new simulation and type the `ts` object name into
your console, do you see a change? Use your knowledge of `ts_samples()` and some
_tidyverse_ table processing to inspect the recorded individuals.**

**Hint:** To make this easier to see, maybe keep the original simulation command
in your script (the one without the `schedule`) but modify it to create a
variable `ts_big` instead.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

```{r}
schedule <- schedule_sampling(
  model,
  times = 0,
  list(p1, 5), list(p2, 5), list(p3, 5), list(p4, 5)
)

# new (smaller) tree-sequence recording
ts <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

# original simulation command (note the missing schedule)
ts_big <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

# see that the new tree sequence is much smaller (even its memory footprint)
ts
ts_big

ts_samples(ts)
ts_samples(ts_big)

ts_samples(ts) %>% group_by(pop) %>% tally()
ts_samples(ts_big) %>% group_by(pop) %>% tally()
```

:::

::: aside

**Note:** In order to make recording of smaller number of individuals from a (potentially huge) number of population easier, `schedule_sampling()` supports a shortcut of `list("all", <number>)` which records the given number of individuals from every population in the model at the given time.

:::

## Exercise: Composing complex recording schedules

What if we need to simulate different number of individuals from different
populations at very specific times? Doing this with a single call to
`schedule_sampling()` is not possible. Luckily, multiple schedules can be easily
combined together into a single sampling schedule.

---

**Type the `schedule` variable in your R console. What do you see? Why did I say
that multiple schedules can be easily combined? And how could we combine them?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

The output of any `schedule_sampling()` function is a plain old data frame! It
contains a bunch of information we used in the `schedule_sampling()` call
(population names, times, etc.), plus a bunch more additional data which is
currently irrelevant.

```{r}
schedule
```

Normally we don't ever have to look at this data (unless something goes wrong
with the sampling, like when a bug in _slendr_ is encountered), but knowing the
format of the schedule means we can easily combine multiple schedules using
standard functions such as `rbind()` (included in base R) or `bind_rows()`
(included in the _tidyverse_ package _dplyr_).

:::

---

In the following chapters, we will be working on implementing many real-world
scenarios from widely established research in population genomics, particularly
those from the field ancient DNA field. Naturally, in cases like this, we need
to be able to simulate sequences of "ancient" individuals as well as various
"present-day" reference panels.

In preparation for these complex exercises, **implement the following sampling
schedules (saving each of them in dedicated, appropriately-named variables),
then bind them together using the function `bind_rows()` mentioned in the
solution to the previous exercise, and simulate a tree sequence `ts` with this
complex schedule, modifying your solution script accordingly.**

| time \n(years B.P.) | population | \# individuals | interpretation
|-------|:-----------|----------------|----------------|
| 0 | p1        | 1              | outgroup individual
|   | p2        | 1              | admixture source
| 0 | p3      | 1              | time-series of ancient individuals
| 0 | p4        | 10              |  reference individuals

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

```{r}

```

---

**Using the function `schedule_sampling` and with the help of `rbind` as shown
in the previous code example, program the sampling of the following sample sets
at given times:**



**Then, schedule the sampling of a single `eur` individual at each of the
following times (i.e., every two thousand years between 40 kya and the
present-day):**

```{r}
t <- seq(40000, 2000, by = -2000)
```

**At the end, bind all individual schedules into a single variable `schedule`
using the function `rbind()`. In total, this should give you a data frame
containing the sampling schedule for the recording of of the genomes of 38
simulated individuals. Verify that this is true by summing the numbers in the 
`n` column of the final data frame `schedule`.**


::: aside
**Note:** You can provide a vector variable (such as `t` in this example) as the
`times =` argument of `schedule_sampling()`.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

First we scheduled the sampling of two Neanderthals at 70kya and 40kya:

```{r}
#| eval: false
nea_samples <- schedule_sampling(model, times = c(70000, 40000), list(nea, 1))
nea_samples # (this function produces a plain old data frame!)
```

Then we schedule one Chimpanzee sample, 5 African samples, and 10 European samples:

```{r}
#| eval: false
present_samples <- schedule_sampling(model, times = 0, list(chimp, 1), list(afr, 5), list(eur, 10))
```

Then we also schedule the recording of one European sample between 50kya and
2kya, every 2000 years:

```{r}
#| eval: false
times <- seq(40000, 2000, by = -2000)
emh_samples <- schedule_sampling(model, times, list(eur, 1))
```

Because those functions produce nothing but a data frame, we can bind
individual sampling schedules together at the end:

```{r}
#| eval: false
schedule <- rbind(nea_samples, present_samples, emh_samples)
schedule
```

Let's verify we scheduled the recording of genomes of everyone we needed:

```{r}
#| eval: false
sum(schedule$n)
```

:::

**Then, verify the correctness of your overall sampling `schedule` by
visualizing it together with your `model` using the function `plot_model()`
(take a look at its manpage `?plot_model` to see how to do this).**

::: aside

**Note:** As you've seen above, the visualization is often a bit wonky and
convoluted with overlapping elements and it can be even worse with samples
added, but try to experiment with arguments to `plot_model` described above to
make the plot a bit more helpful for sanity checking.

:::

```{r}
#| eval: false
plot_model(model, samples = schedule)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

```{r}
plot_model(model, sizes = FALSE, samples = schedule)
```

```{r}
plot_model(model, sizes = FALSE, log = TRUE, samples = schedule)
```
:::

## Exercise 6: Simulating a defined set of individuals

We now have both a compiled _slendr_ `model` and a well-defined sampling
`schedule`, so let's finally simulate some data!

**Use your combined sampling `schedule` to run a new tree-sequence simulation
from your model (again using the `msprime()` function), this time restricted to
just those individuals scheduled for recording. You can do this by running the
following command (note that this also overlays mutations over our genealogies,
which is something we didn't do before).** This will give you a new
tree-sequence object stored in the `ts` variable.

```{r}
#| eval: false
ts <-
  msprime(
    model, sequence_length = 100e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, 
    samples = schedule
  ) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

The command below will likely take a few minutes to run, so feel free to go
down from 100 Mb sequence_length to even 10Mb (it doesn't matter much).
(The `random_seed =` argument is there for reproducibility purposes.)

```{r}
#| eval: false
ts <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 100e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, samples = schedule, random_seed = 1269258439) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8, random_seed = 1269258439)
# Time difference of 2.141642 mins
```


If you're bothered by how long the simulation takes, feel free to call these two lines
to 100% reproduce my results without any expensive computation:

```{r}
#| eval: false
url_path <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bodkan/simgen/refs/heads/main/files/popgen/introgression.trees"
ts_path <- tempfile()
download.file(url_path, destfile = ts_path, mode = "wb")
ts <- ts_read(file = ts_path, model = model)
ts
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: false
# We can save a tree sequence object using a slendr function `ts_write` (this
# can be useful if we want to save the results of a simulation for later use).
if (dir.exists(here::here("files/popgen"))) {
  ts_write(ts, here::here("files/popgen/introgression.trees"))
}
```

**Verify that your simulated `ts` object really does contain only the
explicitly recorded samples, either by typing `ts` into the R console or,
better still, using the function `ts_samples()`.**

::: aside

**Note:** When you think about it, it's quite astonishing how fast _msprime_
and _tskit_ are when dealing with such a huge amount of sequence data from tens
of thousands of individuals on a normal laptop!

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
#### Click to see the solution

Inspect the (_tskit_/Python-based) summary of the new tree sequence
(note the much smaller number of "sample nodes"!):

```{r}
ts
```

Get the table of all recorded samples in the tree sequence;

```{r}
ts_samples(ts)
```

We can also put some _tidyverse_ skills to use and compute the count of
individuals at different time points:

```{r}
library(dplyr)

ts_samples(ts) %>%
  mutate(age_group = if_else(time == 0, "present-day", "ancient")) %>%
  group_by(pop, age_group) %>%
  summarize(n = n()) %>%
  select(age_group, pop, n)
```

:::
